# Authenticate the Glassfrog CLI

Every command that talks to Glassfrog has to prove *who* it is acting as — a
specific organization and person. By the end of this tutorial you will have
stored your API token once, confirmed the CLI can find it on its own, and seen
how it gets attached to outgoing calls so you never manage an auth header by
hand.

You will learn by doing: you will run `glassfrog auth login`, look at the file
it writes, and then watch the CLI pick that token up automatically on later
runs.

## Prerequisites

- The `glassfrog` executable available on your `PATH`.
- A Glassfrog API token for the org + person you want to act as.
- A terminal. (An AI agent or CI job can follow the same steps non-interactively
  — each step notes the scripted equivalent.)

You do **not** need to create or edit any config file by hand. Storing the
token creates it for you.

## Step 1 — Store your token

Run the login command and pass your token as the argument:

```
glassfrog auth login gf_live_yourtoken
```

The CLI writes the token to a credentials file called `.glassfrogrc` in your
home directory and prints where it put it — never the token itself:

```
Stored credentials in /home/you/.glassfrogrc
```

That single line is your confirmation. The token value is deliberately kept out
of the output so it can't leak into terminal scrollback or CI logs.

> **Doing this without a terminal?** Pipe the token on standard input instead of
> typing it as an argument — `printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | glassfrog auth login`. If
> you don't supply a token any other way and you *are* at a terminal, the CLI
> prompts for it without echoing what you type.

## Step 2 — See what got stored

Open the file the CLI just named. It's a small `key=value` text file:

```
# glassfrog credentials
token=gf_live_yourtoken
```

Two things worth noticing:

- The file holds exactly one `token` entry — one token, for one org + person.
- It was created readable only by you (owner-only permissions), because it holds
  a secret.

You won't need to touch this file again. Step 3 shows the CLI reading it for
you.

## Step 3 — Let the CLI find your token automatically

From now on you don't pass the token to anything. When a command needs to
authenticate, the CLI resolves your token at call time by checking, in order:

1. the `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` environment variable,
2. a `.glassfrogrc` in the current directory or any directory above it (the
   nearest one wins),
3. the `.glassfrogrc` in your home directory.

The first source that yields a usable token is the one used. Because you stored
to your home file in Step 1, that's the one that answers — until you introduce a
closer one. The CLI reports *where* the token came from (the file path or "the
environment"), so you can always tell which identity is active, again without
ever printing the secret.

> **Working in automation?** Set `GLASSFROG_TOKEN` in the environment and the
> CLI uses it directly, ahead of any stored file — no file on disk required. An
> empty or whitespace-only value is ignored, and the file search proceeds as
> normal.

## Step 4 — Watch your identity ride along with every call

Once your token is resolved, the CLI attaches it as the `X-Auth-Token` header on
every outgoing Glassfrog API request, exactly as stored — so the API authorizes
the call as you. You don't add the header; it happens for you, once per
invocation, for every request that invocation makes.

The important half of this step is what happens when there is **no** usable
token. The CLI does not quietly send an anonymous request. Instead it refuses to
call the API at all and tells you why:

- **No credentials found anywhere** → it reports that it cannot authenticate
  because no credentials exist.
- **A `.glassfrogrc` exists but can't be read or parsed** → it reports a
  credential error naming that file — a distinct, louder outcome than "no
  credentials," so a broken file is never mistaken for a missing one.

Either way the request is never sent without your identity attached. That's the
safety guarantee: you find out you're not authenticated *before* a call goes
out, not after it returns misleading results.

## What you've learned

- `glassfrog auth login` stores your token once, into `~/.glassfrogrc`, and
  confirms the path without ever echoing the secret.
- The CLI discovers that token automatically on later runs, with a fixed
  precedence: environment variable → nearest project file → home file.
- Your identity is attached to outgoing calls as the `X-Auth-Token` header, and
  the CLI refuses to make anonymous calls when no token is available.
